_status: New test (2026-08-10, PRECISION_GAP_CLOSURE_PLAN.md Tier 2.4 part 2): combines ketamine's activity-dependent NMDA trapping (test_ketamine_activity_dependent.json's mechanism, unchanged) with the fast-spiking interneuron profile at its real-hardware-validated combo (gk_scale=1.0, kinetics_phi=3.0 -- see SimulationEngine.h's fsInterneuronKineticsPhi comment and PRECISION_GAP_CLOSURE_PLAN.md Tier 2.4 part 2 for the ~34.5% baseline separation this produces with no drug present). This is the actual question the fast-spiking work was trying to answer: with a real (if still partial) E/I firing-rate difference now present at baseline, does ketamine's activity-dependent trapping -- which keys off each neuron's own NMDA drive as an activity proxy -- finally produce interneuron > pyramidal block asymmetry, where the flat-profile version (test_ketamine_activity_dependent.json) produced none at all (excitatory and inhibitory suppression tracked within a few hundredths of a Hz at every dose). Compare this file's celltype_rates.csv against test_ketamine_activity_dependent.json's (same doses, same drug mechanism, only the network's intrinsic profile differs) to isolate the fast-spiking profile's effect on ketamine's selectivity specifically.
drug_name: Ketamine (activity-dependent NMDA trapping) + fast-spiking interneuron profile
